questions.q: Find the first four non-zero terms of the Maclaurin series for $f(x)=e^x$, using $f(x)=f(0)+f'(0)x+(f''(0)/2!)x^2+(f'''(0)/3!)x^3+\cdots$.
questions.answer: Since every derivative of $e^x$ equals $e^x$, and $e^0=1$: all derivatives at $0$ equal $1$. So $e^x\approx1+x+x^2/2!+x^3/3!=1+x+x^2/2+x^3/6$.

sections.heading: Using known series to build new ones

questions.q: Using the Maclaurin series for $e^x$, find the Maclaurin series for $e^{-2x}$ up to the term in $x^3$.
Given the Maclaurin series $\sin x\approx x-x^3/6$ and $\cos x\approx1-x^2/2$, find the Maclaurin series for $\tan x$ up to the term in $x^3$, using $\tan x=\sin x/(\cos x)$ and polynomial division.

sections.heading: Using a Maclaurin series to approximate a value

questions.q: Use the Maclaurin series for $e^x$ up to the $x^3$ term to approximate $e^{0.1}$, to four decimal places, and compare with the true value $e^{0.1}\approx1.10517$.
questions.answer: $e^{0.1}\approx1+0.1+(0.1)^2/2+(0.1)^3/6=1+0.1+0.005+0.0001\overline{6}\approx1.1052$. This is very close to the true value $1.10517$, with an error of about $0.00003$.

sections.heading: Tests for convergence of a series

questions.q: Use the ratio test to determine whether the series $1/2+2/4+3/8+4/16+\cdots+n/2^n+\cdots$ converges.
questions.answer: Ratio test: $\lim_{n\to\infty}|a_{n+1}/a_n|=\lim_{n\to\infty}(n+1)/2^{n+1}/(n/2^n)=\lim_{n\to\infty}(n+1)/(2n)=1/2$. Since $1/2<1$, the series converges.

questions.q: Use the ratio test to determine whether the Maclaurin series for $e^x$, $1+x+x^2/2!+x^3/3!+\cdots+x^n/n!+\cdots$, converges for all real $x$.
questions.answer: Ratio test: $\lim_{n\to\infty}|x^{n+1}/(n+1)!/(x^n/n!)|=\lim_{n\to\infty}|x|/(n+1)=0$ for any fixed $x$. Since the limit is $0<1$ regardless of $x$, the series converges for all real values of $x$.

questions.q: Use the ratio test to find the radius of convergence of the power series $x+x^2/2+x^3/3+\cdots+x^n/n+\cdots$.
questions.answer: Ratio test: $\lim_{n\to\infty}|x^{n+1}/(n+1)/(x^n/n)|=\lim_{n\to\infty}n|x|/(n+1)=|x|$. The series converges when $|x|<1$, so the radius of convergence is $R=1$.

questions.q: Find the radius of convergence of the series $1+x+2x^2+6x^3+\cdots+n!\,x^n+\cdots$, and explain what this tells us about where the series is useful.
questions.answer: Ratio test: $\lim_{n\to\infty}|(n+1)!\,x^{n+1}/(n!\,x^n)|=\lim_{n\to\infty}(n+1)|x|=\infty$ for any $x\neq0$. Since this limit is never less than $1$ (except at $x=0$), the radius of convergence is $R=0$ — the series only converges at the single point $x=0$, making it useless as an approximation anywhere else.

sections.heading: Comparing a Maclaurin approximation to the exact function

questions.q: Using the Maclaurin series $\cos x\approx1-x^2/2+x^4/24$, approximate $\cos(0.3)$ to four decimal places, and compare with the true value $\cos(0.3)\approx0.9553$.
questions.answer: $\cos(0.3)\approx1-(0.3)^2/2+(0.3)^4/24=1-0.045+0.0003375\approx0.9553$. This matches the true value to four decimal places, showing the Maclaurin approximation is highly accurate for small $x$.

questions.q: Find the Maclaurin series for $f(x)=\ln(1+x)$ up to the term in $x^4$, using $f(x)=f(0)+f'(0)x+(f''(0)/2!)x^2+(f'''(0)/3!)x^3+(f^{(4)}(0)/4!)x^4$.

sections.heading: Determining the interval of convergence using the ratio test

questions.q: Find the radius of convergence of the Maclaurin series for $\ln(1+x)$, $x-x^2/2+x^3/3-\cdots+(-1)^{n+1}x^n/n+\cdots$, using the ratio test.
questions.answer: Ratio test: $\lim_{n\to\infty}|x^{n+1}/(n+1)/(x^n/n)|=\lim_{n\to\infty}n|x|/(n+1)=|x|$. The series converges when $|x|<1$, so the radius of convergence is $R=1$ (consistent with the earlier result found for a structurally similar series).

questions.q: Using the Maclaurin series $e^x\approx1+x+x^2/2$ and $1/(1-x)\approx1+x+x^2$ (valid for small $x$), find the Maclaurin series for $e^x/(1-x)$ up to the term in $x^2$, by multiplying the two series together.
questions.answer: Multiply term by term, keeping only terms up to $x^2$: $(1+x+x^2/2)(1+x+x^2)=1+x+x^2+x+x^2+x^2/2+O(x^3)=1+2x+5x^2/2+O(x^3)$. So $e^x/(1-x)\approx1+2x+5/2x^2$.

sections.heading: Using differentiation to find a Maclaurin series

questions.q: Given the Maclaurin series $1/(1-x)\approx1+x+x^2+x^3+\cdots$ for $|x|<1$, differentiate both sides term by term to find the Maclaurin series for $1/(1-x)^2$ up to the term in $x^2$.
questions.answer: Differentiating $1/(1-x)$ gives $1/(1-x)^2$ on the left. Differentiating the right side term by term: $d/(dx)(1+x+x^2+x^3+\cdots)=1+2x+3x^2+\cdots$. So $1/(1-x)^2\approx1+2x+3x^2$.

sections.heading: Estimating an error bound in a Maclaurin approximation

questions.q: The Maclaurin series for $\sin x$ truncated after the $x^3$ term is $\sin x\approx x-x^3/6$. Use this to approximate $\sin(0.2)$ to four decimal places, and find the absolute error compared to the true value $\sin(0.2)\approx0.19867$.
questions.answer: $\sin(0.2)\approx0.2-(0.2)^3/6=0.2-0.008/6=0.2-0.001333\approx0.19867$. Absolute error: $|0.19867-0.19867|\approx0.00000$ (to four decimal places), showing that even a low-order Maclaurin approximation is extremely accurate for small values of $x$ close to $0$.

questions.q: Find the first three non-zero terms of the Maclaurin series for $f(x)=(1+x)^{1/2}$, using the binomial series $(1+x)^n\approx1+nx+n(n-1)/2x^2$ with $n=1/2$.
Use the Maclaurin series for $e^x$ up to the $x^4$ term to approximate $\lim_{x\to0}(e^x-1-x)/x^2$, and check that your answer matches the value obtained using L'Hopital's rule.
questions.answer: Using $e^x\approx1+x+x^2/2+x^3/6+\cdots$: $e^x-1-x\approx x^2/2+x^3/6+\cdots$. Dividing by $x^2$: $(e^x-1-x)/x^2\approx1/2+x/6+\cdots$, which tends to $1/2$ as $x\to0$. Using L'Hopital's rule twice on the original limit (since it is initially $0/0$) gives $\lim_{x\to0}(e^x-1)/(2x)=e^0/2=1/2$, confirming the same result.

questions.q: This question has three parts. (a) Find the Maclaurin series for $f(x)=\cos(x^2)$ up to the term in $x^8$, by substituting $x^2$ into the known series $\cos u\approx1-u^2/2+u^4/24$. (b) Use your result to write down an approximation for $\int_0^1\cos(x^2)\,dx$ as a sum of simple fractions (this integral has no elementary closed form, so series approximation is genuinely useful here). (c) Evaluate this approximation as a single decimal, to three decimal places.
questions.answer: (a) Substituting $u=x^2$: $\cos(x^2)\approx1-(x^2)^2/2+(x^2)^4/24=1-x^4/2+x^8/24$. (b) Integrating term by term: $\int(1-x^4/2+x^8/24)dx=x-x^5/10+x^9/216+C$. Evaluating from $x=0$ to $x=1$ gives $1-1/10+1/216$. (c) $1-0.1+0.00463\approx0.905$.

sections.heading: Checking endpoints of an interval of convergence

questions.q: The Maclaurin series for $\ln(1+x)$ has radius of convergence $R=1$ (found earlier in this worksheet). Explain why checking the endpoints $x=1$ and $x=-1$ separately is necessary to determine the full interval of convergence, given that at $x=1$ the series becomes $1-1/2+1/3-1/4+\cdots$ (the alternating harmonic series, which is known to converge).
questions.answer: The ratio test only determines where a power series converges absolutely (the open interval $|x|<1$); it says nothing about the boundary points $x=\pm1$, since the ratio test's limit equals exactly $1$ there (inconclusive), so each endpoint must be checked separately by direct substitution. At $x=1$, the series becomes $1-1/2+1/3-1/4+\cdots$, the alternating harmonic series, which converges by the alternating series test (its terms decrease steadily to $0$). So $x=1$ is included, and the full interval of convergence extends beyond the open interval $|x|<1$ to include this endpoint.

sections.heading: Using a Maclaurin series to evaluate a standard trigonometric limit

questions.q: Use the Maclaurin series for $\sin x$ up to the $x^3$ term to evaluate $\lim_{x\to0}(\sin x)/x$.
questions.answer: Using $\sin x\approx x-x^3/6$: $(\sin x)/x\approx(x-x^3/6)/x=1-x^2/6$. As $x\to0$, this tends to $1$, matching the well-known standard limit $\lim_{x\to0}(\sin x)/x=1$.

sections.heading: Identifying the general term of a Maclaurin series

questions.q: Which of the following is the general term of the Maclaurin series for $\cos x$?
questions.answer: The Maclaurin series for $\cos x$ is $1-x^2/2!+x^4/4!-x^6/6!+\cdots$, which has only even powers of $x$ with alternating signs and factorial denominators matching the power. Checking $(-1)^nx^{2n}/(2n)!$ at $n=0$ gives $1$, at $n=1$ gives $-x^2/2!$, and at $n=2$ gives $x^4/4!$ — all correct. The second option is the general term for $e^x$ with alternating signs, not cosine's even-power structure; the third omits the alternating signs; the fourth describes $\sin x$'s general term, not $\cos x$'s.

sections.heading: Comparing the accuracy of two Maclaurin approximations

questions.q: Both $e^x\approx1+x+x^2/2$ and $\cos x\approx1-x^2/2$ are second-order Maclaurin approximations. Without calculating exact values, explain which approximation is likely more accurate at $x=1$, referencing the size of the next omitted term in each series.
questions.answer: For $e^x$, the next omitted term is $x^3/6$, which at $x=1$ equals $1/6\approx0.167$. For $\cos x$, the next omitted term is $x^4/24$, which at $x=1$ equals $1/24\approx0.042$. Since the cosine approximation's next omitted term is smaller, the $\cos x$ approximation is likely more accurate at $x=1$ than the $e^x$ approximation.
